bibl.title: Quasi-Normal Modes of Stars and Black Holes

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: the complex characteristic frequencies at which a perturbed black hole or relativistic star rings down, and what a detected ringdown could be made to say about the object that produced it
span.quote: In the framework of general relativity (GR) quasi-normal modes (QNM) arise, as perturbations (electromagnetic or gravitational) of stellar or black hole spacetimes. Due to the emission of gravitational waves there are no normal mode oscillations but instead the frequencies become “quasi-normal” (complex), with the real part representing the actual frequency of the oscillation and the imaginary part representing the damping.

span.label: which families of quasi-normal modes exist for black holes and for stars, whether they can be excited and detected, and what the perturbative approach can and cannot establish
span.quote: A critical issue related to the discussions of the previous sections is the excitation of the QNMs. The truth is that, although the QNMs are predicted by our perturbation equations, it is not always clear which ones will be excited and under what initial conditions. As we have already mentioned in the introduction there is an excellent agreement between results obtained from perturbation theory and full nonlinear evolutions of Einstein equations for head-on collisions of two black holes. Still there is a degree of arbitrariness in the definition of initial data for other types of stellar or black hole perturbations. This due to the arbitrariness in specifying the gravitational wave content in the initial data.

span.label: a review of the theory of quasi-normal modes from the mathematical and the astrophysical side at once - the definition via poles of an analytically continued Green function, the families of black hole and stellar modes, the numerical techniques and, unusually, what each of them cannot see
span.quote: In the framework of general relativity (GR) quasi-normal modes (QNM) arise, as perturbations (electromagnetic or gravitational) of stellar or black hole spacetimes. Due to the emission of gravitational waves there are no normal mode oscillations but instead the frequencies become “quasi-normal” (complex), with the real part representing the actual frequency of the oscillation and the imaginary part representing the damping.

span.label: critique
span.quote: Numerical investigations of the fully nonlinear equations of general relativity have provided results which agree with the results of perturbation calculations; in particular numerical studies of the head-on collision of two black holes (cf. Figure 1) and gravitational collapse to a Kerr hole. Recently, Price, Pullin and collaborators have pushed forward the agreement between full nonlinear numerical results and results from perturbation theory for the collision of two black holes. This proves the power of the perturbation approach even in highly nonlinear problems while at the same time indicating its limits.

span.label: ringdown - a compact object losing energy to infinity oscillates at complex frequencies fixed by its own parameters and not by whatever disturbed it
span.quote: Although there are presently several indirect ways of identifying black holes in the universe, gravitational waves emitted by an oscillating black hole will carry a unique fingerprint which would lead to the direct identification of their existence. As we mentioned earlier, gravitational radiation from black hole oscillations exhibits certain characteristic frequencies which are independent of the processes giving rise to these oscillations. These “quasi-normal” frequencies are directly connected to the parameters of the black hole (mass, charge and angular momentum) and for stellar mass black holes are expected to be inside the bandwidth of the constructed gravitational wave detectors.

span.label: linearised Einstein equations decomposed into spherical harmonics, Laplace transformed, with quasi-normal frequencies identified as poles of the analytic continuation of the Green function; then five numerical routes to those poles, each reviewed with the part of the spectrum it cannot reach
span.term: linearised Einstein equations decomposed into spherical harmonics, Laplace transformed, with quasi-normal frequencies identified as poles of the analytic continuation of the Green function; then five numerical routes to those poles, each reviewed with the part of the spectrum it cannot reach
span.quote: A major disadvantage of the evolution schemes is that one cannot get the complete spectrum of the QNMs neither for a star nor for a black hole. The reason is that although any perturbation is the sum of the harmonics involved, in practice only a few of them will be observed and in the best case one can succeed in getting a few extra modes by “playing” around with the initial data. To be more specific, by evolving a perturbation on a black hole background one can get a QNM signal as the one shown in figure 4, but in this signal the Fourier transform will show that there are present at most two frequencies (the slowest damped ones); then by doing “matched filtering” of this signal we will get the right frequencies and damping times, but then all the extra modes of the spectrum are missing!

span.label: the effective potential peaks near the unstable photon orbit at r = 3M; whatever is imposed inside that radius has to cross the peak to reach an observer, and the peak passes only the ringing. This is why the frequencies are a fingerprint of the object rather than of the disturbance, and why a crude close-limit approximation to a black hole collision predicts the waveform correctly
span.term: a barrier that erases the initial data
span.quote: That is, for any set of initial data that one can impose, the QNMs will critically depend on the shape of the potential barrier, and this is the reason that the close limit approximation of the two black-hole collision used by Price and Pullin was so successful, because whatever initial data you provide inside the r < 3M region (the peak of the potential barrier is around 3M) the barrier will “filter” them and an outside observer will observe only the QNM ringing (see for example recent studies by Allen, Camarda and Seidel).

span.label: the quasi-normal frequencies are the zeros of a Wronskian in the analytic continuation of the Green function to Re(s) < 0. The corresponding functions grow exponentially at both ends and are not physical states; what is physical is that they control the late-time decay in any bounded region
span.term: poles of a continuation, not solutions of the problem
span.quote: First of all we should note that because of Re(s) < 0 the function f+ grows exponentially for small and large x! The corresponding spacetime solution is therefore not a physically relevant solution, unlike the normal modes.

span.label: evolving the equations in time and Fourier-transforming the result recovers the modes still present in the signal - the slowest damped ones. Everything with a larger imaginary part has decayed before the window opens, so the method's reach is set by its own arithmetic and not by the spectrum
span.term: a method that can only hear what it does not damp away
span.quote: A major disadvantage of the evolution schemes is that one cannot get the complete spectrum of the QNMs neither for a star nor for a black hole. The reason is that although any perturbation is the sum of the harmonics involved, in practice only a few of them will be observed and in the best case one can succeed in getting a few extra modes by “playing” around with the initial data. To be more specific, by evolving a perturbation on a black hole background one can get a QNM signal as the one shown in figure 4, but in this signal the Fourier transform will show that there are present at most two frequencies (the slowest damped ones); then by doing “matched filtering” of this signal we will get the right frequencies and damping times, but then all the extra modes of the spectrum are missing!

span.label: linearised perturbation theory gives no built-in indication of how good it is; the only quantitative check is to compute the next order and take the difference. So the accuracy of a first-order result is not a property the calculation can report about itself
span.term: an approximation with no internal error estimate
span.quote: A basic feature of linearized perturbation theory is that there is no “built-in” indication of how good the approximation is. But if one has results for a physical quantity to second order in a perturbation parameter, then the difference between the results of the first and second order theory is a quantitative indication of the error in the perturbation calculation. From this point of view second order perturbation theory is a practical tool for calculations.

span.label: whether the late-time solution can be expanded pointwise in quasi-normal modes is unresolved, and has been shown only for one particular potential
span.quote: It is presently unclear whether one can strengthen (16) to a statement like (2), a pointwise expansion of the late time solution in terms of quasi-normal modes. For one particular potential (Pöschl-Teller) this has been shown by Beyer.

span.label: no spectral theorem applies, so the completeness that normal modes enjoy cannot be expected for QNMs
span.quote: Let us finally turn to the “completeness of QNMs”. A general mathematical theorem (spectral theorem) implies that for systems like strings or membranes the general solution can be expanded into a converging sum of normal modes. A similar result can not be expected for QNMs, the reasons are given in section 2.

span.label: properties of quasi-normal modes cannot decide stability; only the appearance of a normal mode settles the question, and then only in the direction of instability
span.quote: If we define stability as boundedness in time for all solutions with data of compact support, properties of quasi-normal modes can not decide the stability issue. However, the appearance of a normal mode proves instability.

span.label: the stability of Kerr is made very plausible but is not established as conclusively as for Schwarzschild, and it is not known whether all solutions stay bounded in time
span.quote: As the Kerr metric outside the horizon (r > r+) is globally hyperbolic, the Cauchy problem for the scalar wave equation (37) is well posed for data on any Cauchy surface. However, the coefficient of ∂2χ/∂φ2 becomes negative in the ergosphere. This implies that the time independent equation we obtain after the Fourier or Laplace transformation is not elliptic! For linear hyperbolic equations with time independent coefficients, we know that solutions determined by data with compact support are bounded by ceγt, where γ is independent of the data. It is not known whether all such solutions are bounded in time, i.e. whether they are stable.

span.label: the Kerr-Newman spectrum has not been calculated at all, because the perturbation equations do not separate
span.quote: The quasi-normal mode frequencies of the Kerr-Newman black hole have not yet been calculated, although they are more general than all other types of perturbation. The reason is the complexity of the perturbation equations and, in particular, their non-separability.

span.label: time-domain evolution cannot return the complete spectrum - at most the two slowest damped frequencies survive into the signal
span.quote: A major disadvantage of the evolution schemes is that one cannot get the complete spectrum of the QNMs neither for a star nor for a black hole. The reason is that although any perturbation is the sum of the harmonics involved, in practice only a few of them will be observed and in the best case one can succeed in getting a few extra modes by “playing” around with the initial data. To be more specific, by evolving a perturbation on a black hole background one can get a QNM signal as the one shown in figure 4, but in this signal the Fourier transform will show that there are present at most two frequencies (the slowest damped ones); then by doing “matched filtering” of this signal we will get the right frequencies and damping times, but then all the extra modes of the spectrum are missing!

span.label: WKB is accurate for low-lying modes and fails for higher-order ones
span.quote: In general with this approach one can calculate quite accurately the low-lying (relatively small imaginary part) QNM modes, but it fails to give accurate results for higher-order modes.

span.label: the continued-fraction method reaches very high mode numbers and, being purely numerical, gives no intuition about the spectrum's properties
span.quote: As a final comment on this excellent method we should point out that it has a disadvantage compared to the WKB based methods in that it is a purely numerical method and it cannot provide much intuition about the properties of the QNM spectrum.

span.label: direct numerical integration for stars cannot reach the w-modes
span.quote: This method is more accurate than the previous one at least in the calculation of the damping times as has been verified in, but still is not appropriate for the calculation of the w-modes.

span.label: the detectors are sensitive in the f-mode band while the p- and w-modes carrying the rest of the information sit above it, and the authors call for detectors in that range
span.quote: For the QNM frequencies of stars, there is a lack of appropriate detectors. Laser interferometers will be sensitive enough in the frequency regime of the f-mode but it will be very hard to detect signals in the frequencies of the p- and w-modes. Nevertheless, from the discussion in section 5 it is apparent that there is a wealth of information in the signal of oscillating neutron stars, and in order to extract this information we need the p- or/and w-modes. This suggests that the ideas considering detectors, or arrays of detectors, in this high frequency regime should be considered more seriously.

span.label: which modes are excited, and by how much, is not determined by the theory - it depends on initial data that are themselves arbitrary until a full nonlinear calculation supplies them
span.quote: A critical issue related to the discussions of the previous sections is the excitation of the QNMs. The truth is that, although the QNMs are predicted by our perturbation equations, it is not always clear which ones will be excited and under what initial conditions. As we have already mentioned in the introduction there is an excellent agreement between results obtained from perturbation theory and full nonlinear evolutions of Einstein equations for head-on collisions of two black holes. Still there is a degree of arbitrariness in the definition of initial data for other types of stellar or black hole perturbations. This due to the arbitrariness in specifying the gravitational wave content in the initial data.

span.label: the energy released as gravitational radiation in stellar collapse is basically unknown, as is its distribution among the modes
span.quote: The discussion in the previous sections has shown that we have an acceptable knowledge of stellar pulsations and that we can extract information from the detection of such oscillations. But as was clear from the discussion earlier in this section, the energy released as gravitational radiation during the stellar collapse is basically unknown. Additionally, it is not known how the energy is distributed in the various fluid and spacetime modes. Both uncertainties depend strongly on the details of gravitational collapse, or in general the mechanism that excites the modes. Unless full 3D general relativistic codes are generated for the gravitational collapse or the final stages of binary coalescence we will never be able to give definite answers to the above questions.

span.label: linearised perturbation theory carries no built-in indication of its own accuracy
span.quote: A basic feature of linearized perturbation theory is that there is no “built-in” indication of how good the approximation is. But if one has results for a physical quantity to second order in a perturbation parameter, then the difference between the results of the first and second order theory is a quantitative indication of the error in the perturbation calculation. From this point of view second order perturbation theory is a practical tool for calculations.

span.label: trapped modes require a star more compact than any realistic equation of state produces, so that family is of no observational relevance
span.quote: The trapped modes exist only for supercompact stars (R ≤ 3M) i.e. when the surface of the star is inside the peak of the gravitational field’s potential barrier. Practically, the first few curvature modes become trapped as the star becomes more and more compact, and even the f-mode shows similar behavior. The trapped modes, as with all the spacetime modes, do not induce any significant fluid motions and there are only a finite number of them (usually less than seven or so). The number of trapped modes increases as the potential well becomes deeper, i.e. with increasing compactness of the star. Their damping is quite slow since the gravitational waves have to penetrate the potential barrier. Their frequencies can be of the order of a few hundred Hz to a few kHz, while their damping times can be of the order of a few tenths of a second. In general no realistic equations of state are known that would allow the formation of a sufficiently compact star for the trapped modes to be relevant.

span.label: whether the algebraically special purely imaginary frequencies are QNMs at all is still questioned
span.quote: The existence of “algebraically special” solutions for perturbations of Schwarzschild, Reissner-Nordström and Kerr black holes were first pointed out by Chandrasekhar. It is still questionable whether these frequencies should be considered as QNMs and there is a suggestion that the potential might become transparent for these frequencies.

span.label: resonance theory from quantum mechanics - alpha decay, poles of a continued Green function, the Bohr-Sommerfeld rule and WKB scattering off a barrier - carried into the calculation of black hole oscillation frequencies
span.quote: In general with this approach one can calculate quite accurately the low-lying (relatively small imaginary part) QNM modes, but it fails to give accurate results for higher-order modes.

span.label: the asteroseismological programme of inferring stellar interiors from an oscillation spectrum, carried from classical astrophysics to neutron stars where the spectrum includes modes of the spacetime
span.quote: From tests performed using polytropic stars to provide data for the above relations it was seen that these equations predict the masses and the radii of the polytropes usually with an error less than 10%. There is work underway towards extracting the parameters of the star from a noisy signal.

span.label: perturbation-theory waveforms compared against fully nonlinear numerical relativity for the head-on collision of two black holes and for collapse to a Kerr hole
span.note: eliminates: the linearised treatment being an artefact of linearisation - the comparison is against a calculation that makes none of its approximations, on the same physical problem · outcome: held

Figure 1) and gravitational collapse to a Kerr hole. This proves the power of the perturbation approach even in highly nonlinear problems while at the same time indicating its limits.

span.label: second-order perturbation theory proposed as the quantitative error estimate for a first-order calculation, since the difference between the orders is the only available measure
span.note: eliminates: a first-order result being reported without any indication of its accuracy - the method has no internal one and the authors say so before proposing this · outcome: partial

But if one has results for a physical quantity to second order in a perturbation parameter, then the difference between the results of the first and second order theory is a quantitative indication of the error in the perturbation calculation. From this point of view second order perturbation theory is a practical tool for calculations.

span.label: five independent numerical routes to the same frequencies - time evolution, integration of the time-independent equation, WKB and phase-integral, continued fractions, and resonance searching - each reported with the part of the spectrum it cannot reach
span.note: eliminates: any one method's blind spot being mistaken for a property of the spectrum; the modes WKB loses are the ones continued fractions find, and vice versa · outcome: held
span.quote: In general with this approach one can calculate quite accurately the low-lying (relatively small imaginary part) QNM modes, but it fails to give accurate results for higher-order modes.

span.label: Nollert's continued-fraction calculation carried to mode number 100,000, on a method whose convergence for quasi-normal modes is not obvious because the relevant solution grows exponentially
span.note: eliminates: the asymptotic mode distribution being an extrapolation from the few modes the other methods reach · outcome: held
span.quote: In the case of quasi-normal modes this is not so clear because f+ grows exponentially. Nevertheless, the method works very well numerically and was improved by Nollert such that he was able to calculate very high mode numbers (up to 100, 000!). In this way he obtained the asymptotic distributions of modes described in (31).

span.label: the potential barrier at r = 3M treated as a filter on initial data, which is why different initial conditions give the same observed ringing
span.note: eliminates: the initial data as an explanation of the ringing - the potential barrier at r = 3M filters whatever is imposed, which is why different initial conditions give the same modes · outcome: absent-declared-unreported
span.quote: That is, for any set of initial data that one can impose, the QNMs will critically depend on the shape of the potential barrier, and this is the reason that the close limit approximation of the two black-hole collision used by Price and Pullin was so successful, because whatever initial data you provide inside the r < 3M region (the peak of the potential barrier is around 3M) the barrier will “filter” them and an outside observer will observe only the QNM ringing (see for example recent studies by Allen, Camarda and Seidel).

span.label: the Cowling approximation, which freezes the spacetime to isolate the fluid modes, and the inverse Cowling approximation, which freezes the fluid to isolate the spacetime modes
span.note: eliminates: the coupling between fluid and spacetime - the Cowling approximation freezes the spacetime to leave the fluid modes alone, and the inverse freezes the fluid to leave the spacetime modes · outcome: absent-declared-unreported
span.quote: From the form of the above equations one can easily see two limiting cases. Let us first assume that the gravitational field is very weak. Then equation and can be omitted (actually S → 0 in the weak field limit) and we find that one equation is enough to describe (with acceptable accuracy) the oscillations of the fluid. This approach is known as the Cowling approximation. Inversely, we can assume that the coupling between the two equations (51) and (52) describing the spacetime perturbations with the equation (53) is weak and consequently derive all the features of the spacetime perturbations from only the two of them. This is what is called the “inverse Cowling approximation” (ICA).

span.label: quasi-normal modes
span.quote: In the framework of general relativity (GR) quasi-normal modes (QNM) arise, as perturbations (electromagnetic or gravitational) of stellar or black hole spacetimes. Due to the emission of gravitational waves there are no normal mode oscillations but instead the frequencies become “quasi-normal” (complex), with the real part representing the actual frequency of the oscillation and the imaginary part representing the damping.

span.label: normal modes
span.quote: First of all we should note that because of Re(s) < 0 the function f+ grows exponentially for small and large x! The corresponding spacetime solution is therefore not a physically relevant solution, unlike the normal modes.

span.label: w-modes
span.quote: Inspired by a simple but instructive model, Kokkotas and Schutz showed the existence of a new family of modes: the w-modes. These are spacetime modes and their properties, although different, are closer to the black hole QNMs than to the standard fluid stellar modes. The main characteristics of the w-modes are high frequencies accompanied with very rapid damping. Furthermore, these modes hardly excite any fluid motion.

span.label: f-mode
span.quote: An important factor for the detection of gravitational waves are the pulsation mode frequencies. Existing resonant gravitational wave detectors, as well as laser interferometric ones which are under construction, are only sensitive in a certain bandwidth. The spherical and bar detectors are typically tuned to 0.6 – 3 kHz, while the interferometers are sensitive within 10 – 2000 Hz. The initial part of the QNM waveform, which carries away whatever deformation a collapse left in the spacetime, is expected to be for a neutron star in the frequency range of 5 – 12 kHz (w-mode). The subsequent part of the waveform is constructed from combination of the f- and p-modes. Still the present gravitational wave detectors are sensitive only in the frequencies of the f-mode.

span.label: trapped modes
span.quote: The trapped modes exist only for supercompact stars (R ≤ 3M) i.e. when the surface of the star is inside the peak of the gravitational field’s potential barrier. Practically, the first few curvature modes become trapped as the star becomes more and more compact, and even the f-mode shows similar behavior. The trapped modes, as with all the spacetime modes, do not induce any significant fluid motions and there are only a finite number of them (usually less than seven or so). The number of trapped modes increases as the potential well becomes deeper, i.e. with increasing compactness of the star. Their damping is quite slow since the gravitational waves have to penetrate the potential barrier. Their frequencies can be of the order of a few hundred Hz to a few kHz, while their damping times can be of the order of a few tenths of a second. In general no realistic equations of state are known that would allow the formation of a sufficiently compact star for the trapped modes to be relevant.

span.label: r-modes
span.quote: Thus, all r-modes with ℓ-mode ≥ 2 are generically unstable to the emission of gravitational radiation, due to the Chandrasekhar-Friedman-Schutz (CFS) mechanism. The instability is active as long as its growth-time is shorter than the damping-time due to the viscosity of neutron star matter. Its effect is to slow down, within a year, a rapidly rotating neutron star to slow rotation rates and this explains why only slowly rotating pulsars are associated with supernova remnants.

span.label: Kerr
span.quote: As the Kerr metric outside the horizon (r > r+) is globally hyperbolic, the Cauchy problem for the scalar wave equation (37) is well posed for data on any Cauchy surface. However, the coefficient of ∂2χ/∂φ2 becomes negative in the ergosphere. This implies that the time independent equation we obtain after the Fourier or Laplace transformation is not elliptic! For linear hyperbolic equations with time independent coefficients, we know that solutions determined by data with compact support are bounded by ceγt, where γ is independent of the data. It is not known whether all such solutions are bounded in time, i.e. whether they are stable.

span.label: completeness
span.quote: Let us finally turn to the “completeness of QNMs”. A general mathematical theorem (spectral theorem) implies that for systems like strings or membranes the general solution can be expanded into a converging sum of normal modes. A similar result can not be expected for QNMs, the reasons are given in section 2.

span.label: potential barrier
span.quote: That is, for any set of initial data that one can impose, the QNMs will critically depend on the shape of the potential barrier, and this is the reason that the close limit approximation of the two black-hole collision used by Price and Pullin was so successful, because whatever initial data you provide inside the r < 3M region (the peak of the potential barrier is around 3M) the barrier will “filter” them and an outside observer will observe only the QNM ringing (see for example recent studies by Allen, Camarda and Seidel).

span.label: evolution schemes
span.quote: A major disadvantage of the evolution schemes is that one cannot get the complete spectrum of the QNMs neither for a star nor for a black hole. The reason is that although any perturbation is the sum of the harmonics involved, in practice only a few of them will be observed and in the best case one can succeed in getting a few extra modes by “playing” around with the initial data. To be more specific, by evolving a perturbation on a black hole background one can get a QNM signal as the one shown in figure 4, but in this signal the Fourier transform will show that there are present at most two frequencies (the slowest damped ones); then by doing “matched filtering” of this signal we will get the right frequencies and damping times, but then all the extra modes of the spectrum are missing!

span.label: quadrupole formula
span.quote: Up to now the general way of calculating the energy emission has been the quadrupole formula. But this formula only accounts for the fluid deformations and motions, and as we have seen this accounts only for a part of the total energy.

span.label: radiative tail
span.quote: The decay of solutions in time is not exponential because of the weak decay of the potential for large r. At late times, the quasi-normal oscillations are swamped by the radiative tail. This tail radiation is of interest in its own right since it originates on the background spacetime.

span.label: the QNM spectrum of a potential - FOR ANY POSITIVE MULTIPLE OF THE REGGE-WHEELER POTENTIAL: an infinite number of modes
span.quote: However this is a delicate issue as we see if, for example, we multiply the Regge-Wheeler potential by a factor ∊: For any ∊ > 0 we obtain an infinite number of QNMs, for ∊ = 0, however there is no QNM!

span.label: the QNM spectrum of a potential - AT MULTIPLIER EXACTLY ZERO: no QNM at all. The count is discontinuous and no precision on the multiplier removes the jump
span.quote: However this is a delicate issue as we see if, for example, we multiply the Regge-Wheeler potential by a factor ∊: For any ∊ > 0 we obtain an infinite number of QNMs, for ∊ = 0, however there is no QNM!

span.label: the spectrum you obtain - BY EVOLVING THE TIME-DEPENDENT EQUATIONS: at most two frequencies, the slowest damped, whatever the initial data
span.quote: A major disadvantage of the evolution schemes is that one cannot get the complete spectrum of the QNMs neither for a star nor for a black hole. The reason is that although any perturbation is the sum of the harmonics involved, in practice only a few of them will be observed and in the best case one can succeed in getting a few extra modes by “playing” around with the initial data. To be more specific, by evolving a perturbation on a black hole background one can get a QNM signal as the one shown in figure 4, but in this signal the Fourier transform will show that there are present at most two frequencies (the slowest damped ones); then by doing “matched filtering” of this signal we will get the right frequencies and damping times, but then all the extra modes of the spectrum are missing!

span.label: the spectrum you obtain - BY CONTINUED FRACTIONS: mode numbers up to 100,000, and no intuition about the spectrum's properties, because the method is purely numerical
span.quote: As a final comment on this excellent method we should point out that it has a disadvantage compared to the WKB based methods in that it is a purely numerical method and it cannot provide much intuition about the properties of the QNM spectrum.

span.label: stellar QNM information - AS THE THEORY OFFERS IT: mass, radius and equation of state to about 10%, IF the f-mode and the first w-mode are both observed
span.quote: From tests performed using polytropic stars to provide data for the above relations it was seen that these equations predict the masses and the radii of the polytropes usually with an error less than 10%. There is work underway towards extracting the parameters of the star from a noisy signal.

span.label: stellar QNM information - AS THE DETECTORS CAN TAKE IT: the f-mode band only; the w-modes sit at 5-12 kHz where the interferometers are not sensitive
span.quote: An important factor for the detection of gravitational waves are the pulsation mode frequencies. Existing resonant gravitational wave detectors, as well as laser interferometric ones which are under construction, are only sensitive in a certain bandwidth. The spherical and bar detectors are typically tuned to 0.6 – 3 kHz, while the interferometers are sensitive within 10 – 2000 Hz. The initial part of the QNM waveform, which carries away whatever deformation a collapse left in the spacetime, is expected to be for a neutron star in the frequency range of 5 – 12 kHz (w-mode). The subsequent part of the waveform is constructed from combination of the f- and p-modes. Still the present gravitational wave detectors are sensitive only in the frequencies of the f-mode.

span.label: what QNM properties settle about stability - AGAINST INSTABILITY: nothing. They cannot decide the issue
span.quote: If we define stability as boundedness in time for all solutions with data of compact support, properties of quasi-normal modes can not decide the stability issue. However, the appearance of a normal mode proves instability.

span.label: what QNM properties settle about stability - FOR INSTABILITY: everything. The appearance of a normal mode proves it
span.quote: If we define stability as boundedness in time for all solutions with data of compact support, properties of quasi-normal modes can not decide the stability issue. However, the appearance of a normal mode proves instability.

span.label: critiques → the quadrupole formula as the route to radiated energy - it accounts only for fluid deformations and misses the emission carried by the spacetime modes
span.quote: Up to now the general way of calculating the energy emission has been the quadrupole formula. But this formula only accounts for the fluid deformations and motions, and as we have seen this accounts only for a part of the total energy.

span.label: critiques → fully relativistic simulation taken on its own - it gives numerical answers without indicating which principles govern the process, and can be simply incorrect or misleading
span.quote: Fully relativistic computer simulations give only numerical answers to problems; often these answers do not provide physical understanding of which principles are important, or even what principles govern a given process. Even more, in some cases, simulation results can be simply incorrect or misleading. By closely coupling various perturbation schemes it is possible to interpret and confirm simulation results.

span.label: qualifies → the perturbative approach itself - the agreement with nonlinear collision calculations proves its power and indicates its limits in the same sentence
span.quote: Numerical investigations of the fully nonlinear equations of general relativity have provided results which agree with the results of perturbation calculations; in particular numerical studies of the head-on collision of two black holes (cf. Figure 1) and gravitational collapse to a Kerr hole. Recently, Price, Pullin and collaborators have pushed forward the agreement between full nonlinear numerical results and results from perturbation theory for the collision of two black holes. This proves the power of the perturbation approach even in highly nonlinear problems while at the same time indicating its limits.

span.label: qualifies → the prospect of neutron-star asteroseismology - the empirical relations recover mass and radius to about 10%, and require observing a mode outside the detectors' band
span.quote: For the QNM frequencies of stars, there is a lack of appropriate detectors. Laser interferometers will be sensitive enough in the frequency regime of the f-mode but it will be very hard to detect signals in the frequencies of the p- and w-modes. Nevertheless, from the discussion in section 5 it is apparent that there is a wealth of information in the signal of oscillating neutron stars, and in order to extract this information we need the p- or/and w-modes. This suggests that the ideas considering detectors, or arrays of detectors, in this high frequency regime should be considered more seriously.

But if one has results for a physical quantity to second order in a perturbation parameter, then the difference between the results of the first and second order theory is a quantitative indication of the error in the perturbation calculation. From this point of view second order perturbation theory is a practical tool for calculations.

Its effect is to slow down, within a year, a rapidly rotating neutron star to slow rotation rates and this explains why only slowly rotating pulsars are associated with supernova remnants.
